PAGE 1

5.3 Solution Curves / Phase Portraits

Summary of \(\vec{x}' = A\vec{x}\)

\(\lambda\)'s Real and Distinct

Linear System:

\[\vec{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & \sqrt{2} \\ \sqrt{2} & -2 \end{bmatrix} \vec{x}\]

Eigenvalues: \(\lambda = -1, -4\)

Eigenvectors:

\[\vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ \sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix} \quad (\lambda = -1), \qquad \vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} -\sqrt{2} \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad (\lambda = -4)\]

\(\leftarrow\) straight line solutions

Phase Plane Dynamics: For two negative eigenvalues (\(\lambda_2 < \lambda_1 < 0\)), both exponential terms decay to zero as \(t \to \infty\). However, \(e^{-4t}\) decays much faster than \(e^{-t}\). Near the origin, the slower-decaying term dominates, causing all non-straight-line trajectories to enter the origin tangent to the eigenvector \([1, \sqrt{2}]^T\) associated with \(\lambda=-1\).

Behavior Near the Origin:

  • Origin corresponds to: \(t = \infty\) (since \(e^{\lambda t} \to 0\) as \(t \to \infty\) if \(\lambda < 0\))
  • At \(t \approx \infty\), \(e^{-t} > e^{-4t}\) (the \(e^{-t}\) term decays slower)
  • So near the origin, solution curves follow the eigenvector of \(\lambda = -1\): \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ \sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix}\)

Equilibrium Point Classification:

The origin is an equilibrium point, specifically an improper nodal sink.

  • Sink: Solutions go into the origin as \(t \to \infty\).
  • Improper Node: Trajectories enter along a single asymptotic direction (tangent to the slower mode) rather than uniformly from all directions.
PAGE 2

Real and Distinct Positive Eigenvalues (Source)

Linear System:

\[\vec{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -1 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \vec{x}\]

Eigenvalues: \(\lambda = 2, 4\)

Eigenvectors:

\[\vec{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} \quad (\lambda = 2), \qquad \vec{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad (\lambda = 4)\]

Source Dynamics: When both eigenvalues are positive (\(0 < \lambda_1 < \lambda_2\)), solutions move away from the origin as \(t \to \infty\). Tracing backwards towards the origin as \(t \to -\infty\), the smaller exponential \(e^{2t}\) is significantly larger than \(e^{4t}\). Therefore, trajectories emerge from the origin tangent to the eigenvector \([1, 3]^T\) associated with \(\lambda=2\).

Behavior Near the Origin:

  • Origin corresponds to: \(t = -\infty\)
  • As \(t \to -\infty\), \(e^{2t} > e^{4t}\) (since \(4t\) becomes more negative faster)
  • Therefore, trajectories leave along the eigenvector direction \(\vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}\) near the origin.

Equilibrium Point Classification:

The origin is an improper nodal source.

  • Source: All trajectories move away from the origin as \(t \to \infty\).
  • Improper Node: Solution curves leave the origin tangent to the slower growth mode eigenvector \([1, 3]^T\).
PAGE 3

\(\lambda\)'s Real and Opposite in Signs

Linear System:

\[\vec{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 4 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \vec{x}\]

Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors:

\[\lambda = 3, \; -1\]\[\vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}, \; \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}\]

Origin is a saddle point

Saddle Point Dynamics: Because the eigenvalues have opposite signs (\(\lambda_1 = 3 > 0\) and \(\lambda_2 = -1 < 0\)), trajectories are attracted toward the origin along the stable line spanned by \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}\) and repelled away from the origin along the unstable line spanned by \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\), forming hyperbolic orbits in the phase plane.

PAGE 4

\(\lambda\)'s Are Repeated

Linear System:

\[\vec{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \vec{x}\]

Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors:

\[\lambda = 1, \; 1\]\[\vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \; \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

(matrix is complete) → not defective

Eigenvalues are equal, so neither eigenvector is more important → solutions are linear combos of both.

Origin is sometimes called a “star node” and is a proper nodal source.

→ no preferred asymptote

Star Node (Proper Nodal Source): When a repeated positive eigenvalue \(\lambda > 0\) has two linearly independent eigenvectors (algebraic multiplicity = geometric multiplicity = 2), every vector in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) is an eigenvector. Trajectories emanate radially straight out from the origin in all directions at the same rate, leaving no curved paths or preferred asymptotic directions.

PAGE 5

Repeated Eigenvalues: Defective Matrix & Improper Nodal Sink

Lecture Notes • Page 5

Linear System Analysis

Differential System:

\[ \vec{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -4 \\ 4 & -7 \end{bmatrix} \vec{x} \]

Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors:

\[ \lambda = -3, -3 \quad (\text{multiplicity } 2) \]

\[ \vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

• Defect of one (only one linearly independent eigenvector)

Defective Eigenvalue Note: When an eigenvalue has an algebraic multiplicity greater than its geometric multiplicity (here, algebraic multiplicity is 2, but there is only 1 independent eigenvector \( \vec{v} \)), the system has a defect of one. This produces only one straight-line solution ray in the phase plane.

Phase Portrait

  • One straight line solution visible: Along the line spanned by the eigenvector \( \vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \) with \( \lambda = -3 < 0 \).
  • Classification: The origin is an improper nodal sink. Trajectories are directed toward the origin as \( t \to \infty \) and enter tangent to the eigenvector line.
PAGE 6

Complex Eigenvalues — Purely Imaginary Case (Center)

Lecture Notes • Page 6

Linear System with Complex Eigenvalues

Differential System:

\[ \vec{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -5 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \vec{x} \]

Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors:

\[ \lambda = i, -i \]

\[ \vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 2+i \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \; \begin{bmatrix} 2-i \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

\( \lambda \)'s are purely imaginary (real part \( \text{Re}(\lambda) = 0 \)), so solution curves are ovals (ellipses).

Determining the Major Axis & Orientation

To find the major axis direction, decompose eigenvector \( \vec{v} \):

\[ \vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 2+i \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}}_{\text{Real part}} + i \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}}_{\text{Imag part}} \]

The sum of the real and imaginary vector components gives the direction of the major axis:

\[ \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

* Incomplete — see next page for full geometric details.

Orientation Test: To find whether the trajectory rotates clockwise or counterclockwise around the center, choose a simple test vector on the axis, such as \( \vec{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \), and evaluate the velocity vector \( \vec{x}' = A \vec{x} \).

Phase Portrait

Classification:

The origin is a center (neutrally stable closed orbits).

Direction Check:

Pick test point: \[ \vec{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \]

Evaluate velocity vector: \[ \vec{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

→ Direction is right, up (counterclockwise motion).

PAGE 7

Ellipse Orientation

Eigenvector Decomposition and Parallelogram

eigenvectors \(\vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + i \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix},\; \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} - i \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\)

form a parallelogram with \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix},\; \pm \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\)

Geometric Interpretation:

For complex conjugate eigenvalues with zero real part (pure imaginary), the solution trajectories form closed elliptical orbits. The axes of the bounding parallelogram are spanned by the real part \(\text{Re}(\vec{v}) = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\) and the imaginary part \(\text{Im}(\vec{v}) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\).

ellipse is inside the parallelogram

PAGE 8

if real part of \(\lambda\) is not zero, then the ovals grow or shrink as they go around

System Analysis and Spiral Dynamics

Linear System

\[\vec{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 5 & -3 \end{bmatrix} \vec{x}\]

Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors

Eigenvalues: \(\lambda = -1+i,\; -1-i\)

Eigenvectors: \(\vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 2+i \\ 5 \end{bmatrix},\; \begin{bmatrix} 2-i \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}\)

Characteristic Equation Breakdown:

For matrix \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 5 & -3 \end{bmatrix}\), \(\text{tr}(A) = 1 - 3 = -2\) and \(\det(A) = 1(-3) - (-1)(5) = 2\). The eigenvalues are roots of \(\lambda^2 - \text{tr}(A)\lambda + \det(A) = \lambda^2 + 2\lambda + 2 = 0\), yielding \(\lambda = -1 \pm i\).

figure out orientation and direction as before

here, real part of \(\lambda\) is negative, so "oval" shrinks as they go

origin is a spiral sink

Stability Summary:

  • \(\text{Re}(\lambda) < 0\): Inward spiral (Spiral Sink / Attractor - Asymptotically Stable)
  • \(\text{Re}(\lambda) > 0\): Outward spiral (Spiral Source / Repeller - Unstable)
  • \(\text{Re}(\lambda) = 0\): Closed elliptical orbits (Center - Neutrally Stable)
PAGE 9

An Unusual Case: One Eigenvalue is Zero

\[ \vec{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \vec{x} \]
\[ \lambda = 0, \, 5 \] \[ \vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \, \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \]

General solution:

\[ \vec{x} = c_1 \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + c_2 e^{5t} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \]

Because \(\lambda = 0\), the term \(e^{0t} = 1\) is static over time. Any multiple of the eigenvector \(\begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\) remains at rest, forming an entire line of equilibria. For \(\lambda = 5 > 0\), trajectories diverge away from this line parallel to \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\).

Geometric Interpretation
